interest: This file provides historians with valuable insights into the regional and structural dynamics of the Japanese banking sector during the Great Depression and the interwar period. It documents the fragility of provincial finance through the Nagoya banking crisis of 1931-1932, the interventionist role of the Bank of Japan, and the fiscal strain of the 1931 gold embargo on major exchange institutions like the Yokohama Specie Bank. Uniquely, the file contains extensive diplomatic correspondence addressing and debunking the persistent Western racial myth that Japanese banks employed Chinese staff due to Japanese dishonesty, contextualizing their employment in technical silver-assaying and foreign exchange traditions. Finally, the cross-reference records track the political tensions surrounding the Bank of Japan's leadership, notably Seihin Ikeda's appointment and subsequent resignation over military spending and policy in China.
overview: This file (894.516) from the Department of State's decimal central files covers financial and banking conditions in Japan from 1930 through 1937. It comprises consular reports, diplomatic despatches, cross-reference sheets, and official correspondence concerning the financial structures and bank panics in Nagoya, the heavy foreign exchange liabilities of the Yokohama Specie Bank following the reimposition of the gold embargo, and the enforcement of the 1932 Law to Prevent the Flight of Capital against foreign diplomats. It also documents an inquiry by an American citizen regarding the myth that Japanese banks employed Chinese nationals due to a lack of commercial honesty, as well as leadership changes at the Bank of Japan, culminating in the resignation of Governor Seihin Ikeda in July 1937 amid escalating military conflict in China.

subfiles.about: A voluntary consular report reviewing the banking facilities, leading financial institutions, and municipal finances of Nagoya, Japan.
subfiles.from: A. R. Preston, American Consul, Nagoya
subfiles.summary: Consul A. R. Preston surveys the commercial banking landscape in Nagoya, highlighting the dominant position of 'Nagoya's Big Three'—the Nagoya Bank, Meiji Bank, and Aichi Bank. The report provides detailed statistics on capitalization, branch offices, and deposit growth since the 1927 financial panic. It also provides an analysis of the ordinary and special municipal budgets of Nagoya City, including tax revenue breakdowns and public debt, noting an outstanding foreign loan underwritten by Lazard Brothers of London.
subfiles.title: Consular Report: Banking Facilities and Finances of Nagoya, Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 458 on the financial losses of the Yokohama Specie Bank.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 458 from Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes in Tokyo, dated January 15, 1932, and filed under 894.00 P.L./49. The dispatch reports on the severe financial losses suffered by the Yokohama Specie Bank following the change of the Japanese Cabinet and the reimposition of the gold embargo.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 458 on Losses of the Yokohama Specie Bank

subfiles.about: An extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 458 reporting on government relief measures for the Yokohama Specie Bank's dollar exchange commitments.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Despatch No. 458 describes how the change of government left the Yokohama Specie Bank with Yen 176,000,000 in dollar exchange contracts at pre-embargo rates. To prevent default, the new Cabinet permitted gold shipments totaling Yen 50,000,000 and transferred Yen 60,000,000 in foreign-currency national bonds held by the Finance Department's Bureau of Deposits. The remaining deficit was to be met through dollar loans from New York banks or loan extensions.
subfiles.title: Despatch Extract: Dollar Commitments and Relief for the Yokohama Specie Bank

subfiles.about: A voluntary consular report detailing a severe banking crisis and runs on major banks in Nagoya.
subfiles.from: J. Holbrook Chapman, American Consul, Nagoya
subfiles.summary: Consul J. Holbrook Chapman reports on acute distress in the Nagoya banking sector following the December 1931 failures of the Koromogaura and Nosho banks. Public anxiety culminated in runs on the Aichi, Nagoya, Meiji, and Murase banks, forcing the Meiji and Murase banks to suspend payments. Intervention by prefectural authorities and the Governor of the Bank of Japan, who pledged Yen 100,000,000 in emergency credit, calmed the runs, though consolidation talks between the Meiji Bank and Aichi Bank remained unresolved.
subfiles.title: Consular Report: Nagoya Banking Situation Disturbed

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 578 on general banking conditions in Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 578 from Tokyo, sent by Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville on April 19, 1932, and filed under 894.50/70. The dispatch provides general reporting on banking conditions and financial developments in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 578 on Banking Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 118 concerning Japanese legal restrictions on foreign currency bank deposits.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 118 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, dated September 8, 1932 (dispatch dated September 6), which was filed under 894.51/379. The communication concerns Japanese legislation that prohibits foreign currency deposits in Japanese banks without prior approval from the Ministry of Finance.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 118 on Foreign Currency Deposits Law

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch transmitting Japanese Foreign Office regulations regarding capital flight and foreign currency bank accounts held by diplomats.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits French and English translations of a Japanese Foreign Office circular note regarding the Law to Prevent the Flight of Capital (Law No. 17) and Finance Ministry Decrees Nos. 12 and 13. Grew reports that the Minister of Finance ruled that members of the diplomatic corps in Tokyo are not exempt from the restrictions on foreign currency accounts. Diplomats are required to submit formal applications through their banks to retain foreign currency deposits, although the Ministry promised to handle them benevolently.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 118: Japanese Law to Prevent the Flight of Capital

subfiles.about: An official French translation of a Japanese Foreign Office circular note and decree regarding foreign currency deposit permits.
subfiles.summary: This circular note from the Japanese Foreign Office informs foreign embassies and legations in Tokyo of the application of Law No. 17 and Ministry of Finance Decrees Nos. 12 and 13. It requests diplomatic personnel to submit formal authorization requests through their banks for foreign currency deposits or loans, promising that the Ministry will examine them favorably to prevent inconvenience. An attached provisional French translation of Article 4 of Decree No. 13 outlines the nine required points of information.
subfiles.title: Enclosure 1 to Despatch 118: French Translation of Foreign Office Circular and Decree
subfiles.to: Foreign Embassies and Legations in Tokyo

subfiles.about: The American Embassy's English translation of the Japanese Foreign Office circular and Article 4 of Decree No. 13 on capital flight restrictions.
subfiles.summary: This document contains the Tokyo Embassy's English translation of the Japanese Foreign Office circular note and Article 4 of Finance Ministry Decree No. 13. It details the procedural requirements for foreign diplomats seeking permission to open or maintain foreign-currency accounts, or borrow/lend foreign money. It lists the nine specific disclosures required on each application, including maximum balances, contract terms, and transaction purposes.
subfiles.title: Enclosure 2 to Despatch 118: English Translation of Foreign Office Circular and Decree

subfiles.about: A diplomatic despatch forwarding Mrs. Wortham James's inquiry on Chinese bank employees in Japan and Ambassador Grew's draft reply.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a letter from Mrs. Wortham James of Newport, Rhode Island, inquiring about the persistent rumor that Japanese banks employ Chinese personnel due to alleged Japanese dishonesty. Grew attaches his proposed reply explaining the legitimate commercial reasons for employing Chinese currency experts and asks the Department to forward it if approved. Noting that Mrs. James requested permission to publish the correspondence in newspapers, Grew emphasizes that he instructed her not to publish his reply.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 967: Transmitting Inquiry of Mrs. Wortham James on Chinese Bank Employees

subfiles.about: A letter from Mrs. Wortham James to Ambassador Grew inquiring whether Japanese banks employ Chinese staff due to Japanese dishonesty.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Wortham James writes from Newport, Rhode Island, asking Ambassador Grew to clarify whether Japanese banks employ Chinese nationals. She recounts hearing since 1905 the rumor that Japanese dishonesty forced banks to use Chinese employees, a claim she had previously refuted after consulting the late Embassy secretary Ransford Miller. Having recently been told by travelers that Chinese employees are indeed visible in Japanese banks, she asks the Embassy for the authoritative truth and requests permission to publish the correspondence.
subfiles.title: Enclosure 1 to Despatch 967: Letter from Mrs. Wortham James to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: A copy of Ambassador Grew's proposed reply explaining that Chinese bank employees are specialized silver and foreign exchange experts.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew explains to Mrs. James that Chinese staff in Japan are employed exclusively in foreign exchange departments of foreign bank branches and certain exchange banks. He explains the historical origin of this practice in Chinese treaty ports, where expert Chinese silver appraisers were essential to test varying coin weights and silver fineness. Grew firmly dismisses the notion that questions of racial honesty dictate bank staffing, confirms that administrative personnel are Japanese, and explicitly requests that his letter not be published.
subfiles.title: Enclosure 3 to Despatch 967: Copy of Ambassador Grew's Reply to Mrs. Wortham James

subfiles.about: The State Department's official reply to Mrs. Wortham James transmitting a revised version of Ambassador Grew's explanation.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Writing on behalf of the Secretary of State, Under Secretary William Phillips provides Mrs. Wortham James with an edited version of Ambassador Grew's statement on bank employment in Japan. The statement explains that Chinese personnel are employed solely for their technical expertise in silver testing and foreign exchange inherited from treaty-port practices, refuting any racial honesty theories. Phillips asks Mrs. James not to publish the letter, while granting permission to use the factual information privately.
subfiles.title: Letter from Under Secretary Phillips to Mrs. Wortham James

subfiles.about: The original unsent draft letter prepared by the Tokyo Embassy for Mrs. Wortham James, superseded by the Department's revised version.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew / Charles E. Finn)
subfiles.summary: This document is the original draft letter from the American Embassy in Tokyo to Mrs. Wortham James, marked 'Not sent See Depts. letter of Oct. 17, 1934'. It contains the initial, unedited text explaining the employment of Chinese exchange clerks and silver experts, which the State Department later revised to remove potentially contentious phrasing. The draft carries the signature 'Charles E. Finn' and concludes with the Embassy's admonition against public publication.
subfiles.title: Unsent Tokyo Embassy Draft Letter to Mrs. Wortham James

subfiles.about: A State Department instruction explaining to Ambassador Grew why his draft letter to Mrs. James was edited prior to transmission.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State acknowledges Despatch No. 967 and explains the modifications made to Ambassador Grew's draft reply to Mrs. James. To avoid misunderstandings surrounding racial controversies, the Department omitted two sentences from the second paragraph and removed permission to attribute the statement to the Embassy. A copy of the revised letter sent to Mrs. James is enclosed for the Embassy's records.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 613: State Department to Ambassador Grew on James Correspondence
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: A letter from Mrs. Wortham James expressing appreciation for the State Department's thorough response and pledging to keep it private.
subfiles.summary: Writing from Maramec Spring near St. James, Missouri, Mrs. Wortham James expresses her gratitude to the Secretary of State for the courteous, prompt, and thorough reply to her inquiry. She promises that the information provided will not be used publicly or published in the press, but notes that she will avail herself of the permission to use the facts privately to correct false impressions.
subfiles.title: Letter of Thanks from Mrs. Wortham James to the Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A State Department instruction transmitting Mrs. Wortham James's letter of appreciation to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Referring to Instruction No. 613 and Despatch No. 967, the Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo a copy of Mrs. Wortham James's letter of October 22, 1934. The enclosed note conveys Mrs. James's appreciation for the thoroughness of the Department's response regarding the employment of Chinese nationals in Japanese banks.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 627: Transmitting Letter of Thanks from Mrs. James to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram on the appointment of Seihin Ikeda as Governor of the Bank of Japan.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Telegram No. 52 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, dated February 10, 1937, and filed under 894.00/693. The telegram reports the appointment of Seihin Ikeda as Governor of the Bank of Japan, succeeding Eigo Fukai who resigned, and includes diplomatic commentary on the political implications of the appointment.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 52 on Appointment of Seihin Ikeda

subfiles.about: A State Department cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum on the resignation of Bank of Japan Governor Seihin Ikeda over China policy.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Far Eastern Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Far Eastern Division, dated July 31, 1937, and filed under 793.94/9145. The memorandum analyzes the resignation of Bank of Japan President/Governor Seihin Ikeda, commenting on the prevailing assumption that his departure stemmed from deep dissatisfaction with Japan's military escalation in China.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Memorandum on Resignation of Seihin Ikeda
